What is a simple machine?

Great question! A simple machine is a tool that makes work easier for us. It helps us lift, cut, pull, or move things with less effort. Simple machines have few or no moving parts. Examples are all around your home: a knife for cutting yam, a bottle opener for opening mineral drinks, scissors for cutting paper, a broom for sweeping, and a wheelbarrow for carrying sand or firewood. Even a spoon can work as a simple machine when you use it to open a milk tin. Machines are our helpers. Look around and count the ones you use daily!

What are the types of simple machines?

Well done for asking! There are six main types of simple machines. The lever, like a crowbar, a see-saw or a bottle opener. The pulley, the wheel with a rope used to draw water from a well or raise our flag on the flagpole. The wheel and axle, found on bicycles, cars and wheelbarrows. The inclined plane, a slope used to roll heavy drums onto a lorry. The wedge, like a knife, an axe or a cutlass that splits and cuts things. And the screw, which holds wood or metal parts firmly together. Each one makes a different kind of work easier. Learn all six!

What is a lever and how does it work?

Good question! A lever is a stiff bar that turns on a fixed point called the fulcrum. When you push down on one end, the other end lifts a load. Think of a see-saw in the playground: the middle support is the fulcrum, and when one child goes down, the other goes up. A bottle opener is a lever; so is a claw hammer removing a nail, and a spoon opening a paint tin. With a long enough lever, a small push can lift a heavy load. That is why levers are such powerful helpers. Try spotting three levers today!

How does a pulley help us draw water from a well?

Lovely question! A pulley is a wheel with a groove where a rope sits. To draw water, the rope passes over the pulley wheel at the top of the well, with a bucket tied to one end. When you pull the rope downwards, the bucket full of water rises upwards. The pulley changes the direction of your pull, so instead of lifting the heavy bucket straight up with your arms, you pull down, which is much easier because your body weight helps you. Pulleys are also used on flagpoles and building cranes. Simple, but very clever!

Why is a knife called a wedge?

Sharp question! A wedge is a simple machine with a thin, sharp edge that splits or separates things when you press or drive it in. A knife is a wedge because its sharp blade pushes into food, like yam or bread, and forces the two sides apart as it cuts. Other wedges include the axe that splits firewood, the cutlass that cuts grass on the farm, a needle piercing cloth, and even your front teeth cutting into an apple! The thinner and sharper the edge, the easier it cuts. That is why we sharpen knives and cutlasses. Well observed!

What is an inclined plane and where do we see it?

Great question! An inclined plane is simply a slope or ramp, a flat surface with one end higher than the other. It makes lifting easier: instead of lifting a heavy load straight up, you push or roll it gently along the slope. Workers roll heavy drums of oil up a plank into a lorry. A ramp beside stairs helps people in wheelchairs enter buildings. Hilly roads that wind around a mountain are inclined planes too, making the climb gradual for cars. Even a ladder leaning on a wall works like one. Slopes turn hard lifting into easier pushing!

Which simple machines can I find in my house and on the farm?

Wonderful question! Your house and farm are full of simple machines. In the kitchen: knives, spoons used to open tins, bottle openers, scissors, and the grinding stone rolling like a wheel. Around the house: door handles, screws holding furniture, brooms working as levers, and the pulley on a well. On the farm: the cutlass and hoe are wedges and levers, the wheelbarrow combines a lever with a wheel and axle, and a ramp of planks helps load produce onto a truck. Make a list of ten machines you find at home and bring it to class!

Why do simple machines make work easier?

Excellent thinking! Simple machines make work easier in three main ways.

First, they can increase your force: a small push on a long lever can lift a heavy stone you could never lift with bare hands.
Second, they can change the direction of your force: with a pulley, you pull down to make a bucket go up, which feels easier.
Third, they can spread the work over a longer distance: pushing a drum up a gentle ramp is easier than lifting it straight up, even though you push for longer. Machines do not remove work; they make it manageable. Clever, right?
